content: Temporomandibular disorders (TMDs) are a group of musculoskeletal conditions that affect the jaw and are often associated with pain that can be challenging to manage. In some cases, this pain may become chronic. Psychological therapies, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), behavior therapy (BT), acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), and mindfulness, aim to help individuals with TMD manage their pain, reduce disability, and alleviate psychological distress. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the effects of psychological therapies in individuals aged 12 years and older who have experienced painful TMD for at least three months. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing psychological therapies to control interventions or alternative treatments, such as oral appliances, medications, or physiotherapy. The search for relevant studies was comprehensive, covering six bibliographic databases up to October 21, 2021, and included both published and unpublished research. The review identified 22 RCTs involving 2001 participants, conducted between 1967 and 2021. Of these, 12 studies were included in meta-analyses. The overall risk of bias in the studies was high, and the certainty of the evidence was judged to be low to very low. The primary outcomes of interest were pain intensity, pain-related disability, adverse events, and psychological distress. The duration of treatments varied, with the shortest being four weeks, and follow-up periods ranged from three to 12 months. Most studies focused on CBT. At the end of treatment, there was no evidence that CBT reduced pain intensity compared to alternative treatments (standardized mean difference [SMD] 0.03, confidence interval [CI] -0.21 to 0.28; P = 0.79; 5 studies, 509 participants) or control interventions (SMD -0.09, CI -0.30 to 0.12; P = 0.41; 6 studies, 577 participants). However, at follow-up, there was evidence of a small benefit of CBT in reducing pain intensity compared to alternative treatments (SMD -0.29, 95% CI -0.50 to -0.08; 5 studies, 475 participants) and control interventions (SMD -0.30, CI -0.51 to -0.09; 6 studies, 639 participants). Regarding pain-related disability, there was no evidence of a difference between CBT and alternative treatments at the end of treatment (SMD 0.15, CI -0.40 to 0.10; P = 0.25; 3 studies, 245 participants) or at follow-up (SMD -0.15, CI -0.42 to 0.12; 3 studies, 245 participants). Similarly, no difference was observed between CBT and control interventions at the end of treatment (SMD 0.02, CI -0.21 to 0.24; P = 0.88; 3 studies, 315 participants) or at follow-up (SMD 0.01, CI -0.61 to 0.64; 2 studies, 240 participants). Adverse events associated with psychological therapies were infrequently reported, and the available data suggested that adverse effects were generally minor and occurred less often than in alternative treatment groups. However, the data were insufficient to draw firm conclusions about the safety of psychological therapies. CBT demonstrated a small benefit in reducing psychological distress at the end of treatment compared to alternative treatments (SMD -0.32, 95% CI -0.50 to -0.15; 6 studies, 553 participants), and this benefit was maintained at follow-up (SMD -0.32, 95% CI -0.51 to -0.13; 6 studies, 516 participants). For CBT compared to control interventions, only one study reported on psychological distress and found no evidence of a difference between groups at the end of treatment (mean difference [MD] 2.36, 95% CI -1.17 to 5.89; 101 participants) or at follow-up (MD -1.02, 95% CI -4.02 to 1.98; 101 participants). The certainty of the evidence was rated as low or very low for all comparisons and outcomes. There was insufficient evidence to draw reliable conclusions about the effectiveness of psychological therapies other than CBT. Additionally, the data were inadequate to determine the potential adverse effects of psychological therapies for painful TMD. In conclusion, the evidence for the effects of psychological therapies on painful TMD is mixed. There is low-certainty evidence that CBT may reduce pain intensity more than alternative treatments or control interventions at the longest follow-up, but not at the end of treatment. CBT may also reduce psychological distress more effectively than alternative treatments, but not control interventions, at both treatment completion and follow-up. However, there is low-certainty evidence that CBT does not improve pain-related disability outcomes compared to other treatments or control interventions. There is insufficient evidence to evaluate other psychological therapies or to determine the safety of psychological interventions for painful TMD. Further research is needed to establish the efficacy of psychological therapies for painful TMD, identify the most effective types of therapy and delivery methods, and determine how these therapies can be best targeted. High-quality RCTs conducted in primary care and community settings are particularly needed. These studies should evaluate a range of psychological approaches, include both adults and adolescents, and measure outcomes such as pain intensity, pain-related disability, and psychological distress for at least 12 months post-treatment.
